citations.quote:
Fix a finite horizon $\tau>0$ and a fixed dimension $p\ge1$. Work on a probability space with an increasing filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le\tau}$ as in [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. For subject $i$, let $T_i$ be an event time, $C_i$ a censoring time, and $Z_i(t)\in\mathbb R^p$ a covariate process predictable relative to this filtration, in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Use the right-censoring record convention of [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]: $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$ and $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$. For this vector covariate process, predictability means coordinatewise predictability: each real-valued coordinate is predictable in the sense of [[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]]. Define the history sigma-algebra $\mathcal G_i:=\sigma\{Z_i(t):0\le t\le\tau\}$. The conditional-independence assumption is $T_i\perp\!\!\!\perp C_i\mid\mathcal G_i$, meaning that for all bounded measurable real functions $a,b$, $E[a(T_i)b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]=E[a(T_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]E[b(C_i)\mid\mathcal G_i]$ almost surely, as in [[def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. This conditional-independence relation is a model assumption, not an empirical conclusion. No conditional-kernel representation given the entire covariate path is assumed here.

A Cox proportional-hazards specification fixes a coefficient $\beta_0\in\mathbb R^p$ and a baseline hazard density $\lambda_0:[0,\tau]\to[0,\infty)$ that is measurable and integrable. Its baseline cumulative hazard is the absolutely continuous function
$$ \Lambda_0(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_0(u)\,du. $$
The conditional event intensity at time $t$ for subject $i$, while that subject is at risk, is
$$ Y_i(t)\lambda_0(t)\exp\{\beta_0^T Z_i(t)\},\qquad Y_i(t):=1\{U_i\ge t\}. $$
These specify the conditional event-intensity component. The law of the covariate paths and the censoring law subject to the stated conditional-independence assumption remain nuisance components and are not fixed here. Thus this is a semiparametric model specification; $(\beta_0,\lambda_0)$ alone do not define a full parametric statistical experiment on the observed-data space.
For the counting-process arguments below, require $Y_i$ to be predictable as well; this is part of the stated observation model and is not inferred from the hazard formula alone.
For a constant covariate value $z$, the corresponding event survival function is
$$ S(t\mid z)=\exp\{-e^{\beta_0^Tz}\Lambda_0(t)\}. $$
For fixed covariate values $z,z'\in\mathbb R^p$, at times with $\lambda_0(t)>0$ the hazard ratio is
$$ \frac{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz}}{\lambda_0(t)e^{\beta^Tz'}}=e^{\beta^T(z-z')}. $$
The relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z-z')}$ even at times when both baseline-scaled hazards vanish and their quotient is undefined. It is an instantaneous hazard ratio, not a ratio of cumulative event probabilities. For time-varying covariate paths $z(t),z'(t)$ the instantaneous relative hazard factor is $e^{\beta^T(z(t)-z'(t))}$ and may vary with time.

For a sample of $n$ subjects, put $R(t)=\{j:U_j\ge t\}$. When failures are untied, the Cox partial likelihood on $[0,\tau]$ is
$$ L_p(\beta)=\prod_{i:\,\delta_i=1,\ U_i\le\tau} \frac{\exp\{\beta^TZ_i(U_i)\}}{\sum_{j\in R(U_i)}\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(U_i)\}}. $$
An empty product is $1$. This partial likelihood is built from risk-set contributions; it is not asserted to be the full likelihood of the censored observations.

Tied-event likelihoods require an explicit time-recording convention. Put $D(t)=\{i:U_i=t,\delta_i=1\}$ and $d_t=|D(t)|$. If a discrete or grouped-time model conditions on exactly $d_t$ failures from $D(t)\subseteq R(t)$ at recorded time $t$ with the risk set fixed for that time, additionally assume that, conditional on that risk set, its covariate weights, and $d_t=d$, the failure subset law assigns each size-$d$ set $A\subseteq R(t)$ probability proportional to $\prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)$. Under this explicit subset-law assumption, its exact conditional tie contribution is
$$ \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq R(t)\\|A|=d_t}}\ \prod_{j\in A}w_j(t)}, \qquad w_j(t):=\exp\{\beta^TZ_j(t)\}. $$
For the separate exact Cox tied-partial-likelihood convention obtained by coarsening a continuous-time ordering into one recorded tie interval, assume the risk set at the interval start is $R(t)$, its only within-interval departures are the $d_t$ failures in $D(t)$, and the covariates are fixed at the recorded time. Conditional on each successive failure, the next failure label is chosen from the remaining risk set with probability proportional to its weight. Summing these order contributions gives the ordered-risk-set conditional partial-likelihood contribution
$$ \sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))} \prod_{k=1}^{d_t} \frac{w_{\pi_k}(t)} {\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\sum_{\ell<k}w_{\pi_\ell}(t)}. $$
Here $\operatorname{Perm}(D(t))$ is the set of bijections from $\{1,\ldots,d_t\}$ to $D(t)$.
The discrete subset expression is exact under its explicit subset-law convention, and the permutation expression is exact for its stated partial-likelihood ordering convention; the latter is not generally the full likelihood of interval-coarsened censored observations. These conventions are not interchangeable without a model relating them. The Breslow and Efron tie formulas are approximations, respectively
$$ L_B(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)\right)^{d_t}} $$
and
$$ L_E(\beta)=\prod_{t:d_t>0} \frac{\prod_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)} {\prod_{k=0}^{d_t-1}\left(\sum_{j\in R(t)}w_j(t)-\frac{k}{d_t}\sum_{i\in D(t)}w_i(t)\right)}. $$
With an absolutely continuous event hazard and independent subjects, exact event-time ties have probability zero; grouped-time tie formulas describe additional observation/model conventions.

For a discrete event-time law, the survival relation $S(t\mid z)=S_0(t)^{e^{\beta^Tz}}$ describes proportional integrated hazards and is not equivalent in general to a hazard-ratio model. The proportional-hazards and proportional-integrated-hazards formulations agree under the continuity condition on the baseline survival; the hazard-density model above uses the absolutely continuous convention.

The counting-process martingale property used for inference is a separate model-contract assumption in the estimator theorem below. The hazard formula by itself does not assert that a compensated event count is a martingale. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the cited event-observation and predictability interfaces; this definition makes no further choice.

Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

Use the empirical-measure convention of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]]: for iid observations $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ with common law $P$, $P_nf=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)$ and $Pf=\int f\,dP$. Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty class of measurable real-valued functions with a nonnegative measurable integrable envelope $F$, meaning $|f|\le F$ $P$-almost surely for every $f\in\mathcal F$ and $PF<\infty$. It is **pointwise measurable** if there is a countable subclass $\mathcal F_0$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ is the pointwise limit of a sequence from $\mathcal F_0$. For a pointwise-measurable class, dominated convergence [[thm-dominated-convergence]] gives $Pf_k\to Pf$ along the approximating sequence, and finite empirical averages converge pointwise, so the supremum defining the uniform law is determined by $\mathcal F_0$. The class is **$P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if

$$\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\longrightarrow0$$

in probability. It is **strongly $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli** if the same convergence holds almost surely. For an uncountable class with a countable pointwise-dense subclass, the supremum is interpreted using outer probability unless the chosen version makes it measurable. For a pointwise-measurable class the supremum is determined by the countable subclass and is measurable. That subclass has a common conull envelope bound, so the supremum is finite almost surely; after choosing a real-valued version, almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability by [[thm-almost-sure-convergence-implies-convergence-in-probability]].

Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a nonnegative integrable envelope $F$. Suppose $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^1(P))<\infty$ for every $\epsilon>0$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Glivenko–Cantelli: $\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|P_nf-Pf|\to0$ in probability. If Countable Choice is assumed, then the stronger conclusion holds that this convergence is almost sure. The terms $P_n$, $P$, and the outer-probability convention are those of [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]], and the class notion is [[def-glivenko-cantelli-class]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Put $R=\sup_{\beta\in B}\|\beta\|_2$ and $C=e^{KR}\max(1,K,K^2)$. Each risk coordinate is bounded by $C$ and is Lipschitz in $\beta$ with constant at most $KC$, since the segment between two points of $B$ lies in the radius-$R$ ball. By [F6]–[F7], the expectations are jointly measurable in time and parameter. Both empirical and population functions are continuous in parameter, so each parameter supremum equals the supremum over a fixed countable dense subset of $B$ and is measurable. Population ratios are deterministic Borel time functions and hence predictable.

For each fixed $t,\beta$ and coordinate $f$, independence and centering give $E[(P_nf-Pf)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(f)/n\le C^2/n$: the cross terms vanish by independence. On a finite $\varepsilon$-net of $B$, the squared maximum over its $m_\varepsilon$ points and the $d=1+p+p^2$ coordinates has expectation at most $dm_\varepsilon C^2/n$. Between a point and its nearest net point, the empirical-minus-population Lipschitz bound is $2KC\varepsilon$. Thus $\limsup_n E D_n(t)^2\le8K^2C^2\varepsilon^2$; let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. The uniform bound $D_n\le2C$ and [F8] applied to $t\mapsto E D_n(t)^2$, followed by [F7], prove $E\int D_n^2d\nu\to0$.

Write $q=P(U_i\ge\tau)$. Since $c_0\le s^{(0)}(\tau,\beta_0)\le e^{K\|\beta_0\|_2}q$, $q>0$. For $Q_n=n^{-1}\sum_i1\{U_i\ge\tau\}$, independence gives $E(Q_n-q)^2=q(1-q)/n$, so $P(Q_n<q/2)\le4(1-q)/(nq)\to0$. Monotonicity of $Y_i$ and the weight bound give $S_n^{(0)}(t,\beta)\ge e^{-KR}Q_n$ for every $t,\beta$. Hence on the event $E_n=\{Q_n\ge q/2\}$ all sample denominators are at least $c=e^{-KR}q/2$, while all population denominators are at least $e^{-KR}q$.

On $E_n$, ratio subtraction and the bounds of steps 1.1 and 3.1 bound both $\sup_B\|\bar Z_n-\bar z\|_2$ and $\sup_B\|V_n-V\|_{\max}$ by a constant times $D_n(t)$. Off $E_n$, the weighted means have norm at most $K$ and the second-moment matrices have entries at most $K^2$, including the zero convention, so both errors remain bounded by constants depending only on $K,p$. Their expected squared errors are therefore at most $C_1E D_n(t)^2+C_2P(E_n^c)$. Steps 2.1–3.1 prove the fixed-time conclusions; integration against finite $\nu$, or [F7]–[F8], proves their integrated versions.

Under [A1], each coordinate class has the envelope from step 1.1 and the hypotheses of [F3]–[F5]. Apply only the probability branch of [F5] and take the finite union over coordinates to obtain $\sup_tD_n(t)\to_P0$. Step 4.1's ratio bound on $E_n$, whose probability tends to one, gives both uniform-in-time ratio conclusions. No such time-indexed class hypothesis was used in steps 1.1–4.1.
